title: Delivering your pēpi
description:
There are several ways to deliver your pēpi. The appropriate approach depends on your personal preferences, your health status, and the medical needs of your pregnancy.

Please be assured that choosing the delivery method is a shared decision-making process between mum, their partner, and whānau, and the certified healthcare providers (e.g., a midwife, a leading maternity carer (LMC), or an obstetrician). They will be present throughout your pregnancy, and at your labour to support you through birth.

This process personalises birthing to the individual and ensures that the best and most appropriate care is provided to mums and their whānau.

contentSections.title: Spontaneous
contentSections.content: Labour and muscle contractions begin naturally to open mum's cervix between weeks 37 and 40. Pēpi is delivered through the vagina without medical intervention or surgical tools. This is the standard approach for giving birth if there are no health concerns for mum or pēpi.

contentSections.title: C-Section
contentSections.content:
This is an operation where a cut is made through your abdomen and womb to deliver the pēpi. It is advised that you discuss this with the LMC to determine whether this option is appropriate.

In most cases, C-Sections are only recommended when medically necessary, as covered in the Pregnancy Complications section.

contentSections.title: What happens if there are health complications?
contentSections.content:
If either mum or pēpi has a health problem, e.g. Gestational diabetes, Pre-eclampsia, or that pēpi is overdue, alternative delivery methods are considered and often recommended by doctors.

The two most prominent methods are an induced labour or a C-section, which you can read more about in the Pregnancy Complications section.
